topic: Food Safety, Food Science and Special Diets
subject: food-technology

items.title: The MSG 'syndrome' myth
items.claim: The idea that monosodium glutamate causes a distinctive 'Chinese restaurant syndrome' came from a 1968 letter to the New England Journal of Medicine. What does the controlled evidence show?

options.text: Robust evidence MSG causes the symptoms in most people
Double-blind trials have not consistently linked MSG within typical food levels to the reported symptoms
MSG is toxic at any dose

items.reveal_title: The popular reaction outran the evidence
items.reveal:
Reviews including the US Food and Drug Administration's classification of MSG as 'Generally Recognised As Safe' (GRAS) and double-blind challenge studies have not consistently reproduced the symptoms at dietary doses.

Kikunae Ikeda first isolated glutamate as the source of umami in 1908 at Tokyo Imperial University.
items.why: A high-profile anecdote can shape food policy and public perception for decades.

items.title: The cold chain's wider effect
items.claim: Mechanical refrigeration became common in 20th-century homes and supply chains. Beyond food preservation, what is one less-obvious effect?

options.text: It made beef cheaper to ship from Argentina to Europe, restructuring agriculture in both regions
It eliminated the need for canning

items.reveal:
Refrigerated ships from the 1880s onwards allowed Argentine, Australian and New Zealand meat exports to Britain, reshaping rural economies and diets.

Domestic refrigerators became common in US homes in the 1930s-1950s and in the UK from the 1960s.
items.why: Food technologies reorganise economies, not just kitchens.

items.title: Why we cure meat with nitrites
items.claim: Sodium nitrite is used in cured meats partly for colour and flavour. What is its main food-safety function?
items.reveal:
C. botulinum produces one of the most lethal toxins known. Nitrites suppress its growth in the anaerobic conditions inside cured meats.

The IARC classified processed meat as Group 1 carcinogenic to humans in 2015 partly due to nitrite and nitrate residues; risks and benefits are now actively traded off in regulation.
items.why: Food additives often combine functional safety roles with health trade-offs.
